title: Al-Kindi, the philosopher
hookLine: the philosopher of the Arabs, who wrote on optics, music and code-breaking

cards: A letter arrives, and every word is scrambled. The letters have been swapped for others by a secret rule, and you don't know the rule. Where do you even start?
A scholar in Baghdad wrote down an answer. Count how often each letter appears in a long ordinary text in the same language. Then count the signs in the secret message.
The sign that shows up most is probably standing in for the letter that shows up most in ordinary writing. Match them up, one by one, and the message begins to open.
The man who wrote that method also wrote on light, on music, and on God. His name was al-Kindi.

teach.h: A TITLE: PHILOSOPHER OF THE ARABS.
teach.b: Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi worked in Baghdad in the age of the House of Wisdom, when Greek books were being turned into Arabic. Later writers gave him a title: the philosopher of the Arabs.
He wrote philosophy in Arabic, using the new translations, asking the old Greek questions in the language of the Qur'an. His range is the first surprise.
Optics: how rays travel and how we see. Music: the strings of the oud and how notes fit together. Medicine, the tides, swords and perfumes, and breaking codes, as in the hook.
The second surprise is how he defends the whole project. Some people in his day were suspicious of learning that came from the Greeks.
Al-Kindi answered, in his book on first philosophy: we should not be ashamed to welcome the truth and take it in, wherever it comes from, even from distant peoples.
The truth, he says, does not make the one who seeks it smaller. It honors him.
And he wrote that philosophy at its highest is knowing the true One, the cause of all things.

For al-Kindi, reason and faith in one God were meant to walk the same road. Muslim thinkers after him took different positions on how far philosophy should go, and that argument comes later in the path.
Today, just meet one of its early voices.

how: Muslim students of philosophy read al-Kindi as an early thinker who wrote philosophy in Arabic and held that reason and belief in one God could work together.

games.q: you're holding a secret letter. every letter has been swapped by a rule you don't know. what do you do first?
o: count how often each sign appears.
games.why: al-Kindi's method: count the signs, compare with how often letters appear in ordinary writing, and match them up.

practice: Hold one small fact from today that you didn't know, maybe that a philosopher broke codes by counting letters, and turn it over: where did it come from, and who first noticed it?
Then let your mind rest on al-Kindi's idea: welcome the truth, wherever it comes from. If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you learned this week; if not, just be glad of it.
